legend: Inflammatory bowel disease associated dysplasia. This example of ulcerative colitis-associated dysplasia, hypermucinous pattern, shows both low- and high-grade dysplasia.

diagnosis: Inflammatory bowel disease–associated dysplasia of the colorectum, intestinal type
legend: Low-grade dysplasia, with slender, hyperchromatic, crowded nuclei aligned along the cell bases and extending to the epithelial surface; goblet cells are sparse, and their mucin vacuoles are frequently small.

diagnosis: Inflammatory bowel disease–associated dysplasia of the colorectum, intestinal type
legend: High-grade dysplasia with hyperchromatic, pleomorphic nuclei, stratified haphazardly within the cytoplasm.

diagnosis: Inflammatory bowel disease–associated dysplasia of the colorectum, serrated type
legend: Low-grade dysplasia with serrated crypts lined by columnar and goblet cells with non-stratified hyperchromatic, crowded nuclei.

diagnosis: Inflammatory bowel disease–associated dysplasia of the colorectum, serrated type
legend: High-grade dysplasia with serrated crypts lined by columnar cells with eosinophilic cytoplasm and enlarged, haphazardly stratified nuclei.

diagnosis: Inflammatory bowel disease–associated dysplasia of the colorectum

legend: A Low-grade conventional (adenomatous) dysplasia demonstrates mildly enlarged, pseudostratified, pencil-shaped, hyperchromatic, crowded nuclei involving both the crypts and surface epithelium.
B High-grade conventional (adenomatous) dysplasia is characterized by severe cytological and architectural atypia, including cribriform growth.
This is characterized by the presence of dysplasia limited to the basal portions of the crypts, without surface involvement. This case shows low-grade (adenomatous) dysplasia.
source: Courtesy of Dr. Penny McKelvie at St. Vincent's Hospital Melbourne, Australia

legend: C Goblet cell–deficient dysplasia. This dysplasia is characterized by a complete absence of goblet cells, instead showing cells with enterocyte-like eosinophilic cytoplasm. Mild nuclear atypia is present in both the crypts and surface epithelium.

D Crypt cell dysplasia. This dysplasia is characterized by a non-crowded, flat, tubular growth pattern, with crypts lined by enterocytes and interspersed goblet cells in roughly equal proportions. The cell nuclei are mildly enlarged, hyperchromatic, mostly round to oval, and non-stratified. The atypical cells extend to the surface epithelium.

B Hypermucinous dysplasia. This dysplasia demonstrates tall columnar cells with multilayered mucin caps with small hyperchromatic nuclei pushed to the base. The dysplastic nature of the nuclei is more easily discernible at the crypt bases.

diagnosis: Sessile serrated lesion–like lesion with focal low-grade dysplasia
legend: This type of lesion is characterized by sessile serrated lesion features (seen in the middle of the image) with a focal region of conventional adenomatous dysplasia (top left).

This lesion demonstrates a tubulovillous growth pattern, characterized by low-grade columnar cells with eosinophilic cytoplasm, slit-like serrations, and ectopic crypts. This lesion appears identical to its sporadic counterpart.

A Serrated dysplasia NOS. A non-exophytic serrated lesion with diffuse marked nuclear dysplastic epithelial changes. Based on the degree of nuclear atypia, loss of nuclear polarity, and nuclear stratification, this is categorized as high-grade dysplasia.
